title: Learning from one stream
hook: each stream keeps some treasure well

segments.voice: Yesterday, visiting another stream: shoes off, head covered, cupped hands for karah prashad. Your line was courtesy is enough. Whose custom did you keep? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

A grandmother keeps the family's pickle recipe. An uncle remembers which villages the family came from. A cousin is the only one who still plays the harmonium properly. Nobody holds everything. Lose one of them and something goes quiet in the family. The panth works a bit like that. Over this block, stream after stream turned out to be guarding something particular. Today asks what each one keeps, and what anyone might borrow.
screen: `A RECIPE, A MAP, A HARMONIUM.` → `NOBODY HOLDS EVERYTHING.` → `WHAT DOES EACH STREAM KEEP?`

segments.voice: Walk back through the streams and look for the treasure each keeps well. The Nihangs keep the old warrior dress, the martial art of gatka, and a playful, defiant way of speaking. The taksals keep pronunciation: students learn to read Gurbani slowly, syllable by syllable, so that the Guru's words come out whole. The Nirmalas keep learning, scholars reading widely and explaining the Granth. The Udasis keep a life of renunciation and care for shrines. The Namdharis keep simplicity, white dress, and kirtan sung in the old ragas. The gurmat sangeet schools keep those ragas alive for everyone. Sikh Dharma sangats in the West keep early-morning practice, and some Western sangats explain things in English for newcomers. The rababis kept music at the Harmandir, and the dhadis keep history in the voice. Not one of these is the whole panth. Each keeps a corner of the house well lit. Gurbani gives an image for this. In Raag Suhi, around Ang 765, Guru Nanak speaks of a box of virtues: if someone has one, open it and enjoy its fragrance; and if a friend has virtues, become partners in them, and leave faults behind. That's the posture of learning from a stream. You don't have to join it, or agree with it on everything. You can borrow its fragrance: a slower way of reading, an earlier hour, a raga, a straighter back. The streams don't lose anything by sharing. That's how a fragrance works.
screen: `NIHANGS, TAKSALS, NIRMALAS, UDASIS.` · `NAMDHARIS, RAGAS, WESTERN SANGATS.` · `A BOX OF VIRTUES, OPENED.` · `BORROW THE FRAGRANCE.` · then, large: `EACH KEEPS A TREASURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take one practice from a stream. Settle, and breathe. Go through the list once more, slowly: gatka, careful pronunciation, study, simplicity, ragas, the early morning, history in song. Notice which one your attention lands on. Don't overthink it. Then make it small: read one line of Gurbani slowly, syllable by syllable; wake a little earlier tomorrow; listen to one shabad sung in its raga. Breathe with the choice, and let it stay small. The bell holds the time.
Learning from one stream. Each stream of the panth keeps some treasure well, and anyone can borrow its fragrance without leaving their own. Today's word.
Your line: each keeps a treasure. Today, try the one practice you chose, even for five minutes, and notice what it gives you. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Sikhs learn from a stream other than their own: practicing gatka with Nihangs, learning pronunciation through taksal teaching, studying raga kirtan at gurmat sangeet schools, or joining early-morning programs in Western sangats.

fork.setup: you're Guru Nanak, speaking of a friend who has virtues you lack. what do you suggest?
options: become partners in virtues, and leave faults behind.
ignore them and keep your own ways.
fork.reveal: in Raag Suhi he speaks of opening the box of virtues and sharing its fragrance. learning from another stream works the same way.

original.note: Punjabi: a school or lineage of teaching within the panth.

trapdoor: what you thought: the streams of the panth are rival camps.
what it means: each stream keeps some treasure well, and others can learn from it.
what a scholar hears: Guru Nanak's box of virtues in Raag Suhi: open it, share its fragrance, become partners in virtue.

notes: Ang 765–766 'gunaa kaa hovai vaasulaa kadh vaas laeejai, je gun hovan saajanaa mil saajh kareejai' paraphrased as a box of virtues opened for its fragrance, and becoming partners in virtues while leaving faults. Please confirm Ang and paraphrase.

Summaries of each stream (Nihang dress and gatka; taksal pronunciation; Nirmala learning; Udasi renunciation and care of shrines; Namdhari simplicity and raga kirtan; Western sangats' early practice and English explanation; rababis and dhadis) follow earlier Block F days. Please confirm each is fair; past tense is used only for the rababis at the Harmandir.
